detail:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) describes gout management as having two parts: treating the inflammation and pain of an acute flare, and lowering uric acid over the long term to prevent future flares and joint damage. The CDC notes that clinicians may use medicine classes such as nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), corticosteroids, and other anti-inflammatory agents for flares, and urate-lowering therapies for people with recurrent flares or other indications, with choices guided by kidney function, other conditions, and medicines already in use.

The CDC also describes lifestyle measures as part of many care plans, including limiting alcohol, limiting foods and drinks high in purines or added sugars, maintaining a healthy weight, and staying hydrated, alongside management of conditions that often occur with gout such as high blood pressure, diabetes, and kidney disease. Sources describe follow-up that tracks flare frequency and, for people on urate-lowering therapy, blood uric acid levels over time, since reaching and holding a target level is associated in sources with fewer flares and shrinking crystal deposits.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about managing gout and uric acid levels.
sourceName: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
summary: The CDC describes gout management in two parts, treating acute flares with anti-inflammatory medicine classes and lowering uric acid long term, alongside lifestyle measures and care for related conditions.
takeaways: care plans address both acute flares and long-term uric acid levels
lifestyle measures and related conditions are part of many care plans
never start, stop, or change medicines without your doctor
title: Gout: managing flares and lowering uric acid day to day
